title: Listening to a bridge
bodyMd:
For most of the twentieth century, a bridge was checked the way a doctor once checked a patient: by looking. Inspectors walked the deck, climbed among the girders and noted cracks, rust stains and loose bolts, usually once every few years. The method had obvious limits. It saw only surfaces, it depended on the eye and experience of whoever happened to be inspecting, and it caught a problem only if the problem was visible on the day of the visit.

Permanent monitoring promised to close those gaps. Strain gauges bonded to the steel, tilt meters on the piers and accelerometers that record how the deck vibrates under traffic can report day and night, in all weathers. When a regional road authority fitted its longest river crossing, a 640-metre girder bridge, with some 350 sensors, its engineers expected to hear of trouble months before any inspector could have seen it.

What they heard first was how much a healthy bridge moves. The deck grew and shrank by several centimetres between a winter night and a summer afternoon; its natural frequencies of vibration drifted with temperature; a single overloaded lorry produced strain readings that, on paper, looked alarming. In its first year the system raised more than two thousand alerts, almost all of them caused by weather and traffic rather than by damage. The engineers began to ignore the alarms, which is the one response an alarm must never invite.

The cure was not more sensors but a better idea of normal. Over several years the team built a record of how each reading varied with temperature, season and load, and set its alerts against that shifting baseline instead of against fixed limits. The alerts fell to a handful a year, and each one was now worth reading. The inspectors, meanwhile, kept their jobs. A sensor can report that something has changed; someone still has to go and see what it is.
